title: The Most Valuable Thing I Got From College Was Free
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Prompted by her youngest child's graduation, Mulder argues that the most formative education she received at university came from outside the curriculum. The catalyst was a communication class taught by a man in his seventies, a working talent agent rather than a professor, whose class changed everything for her precisely because it did not follow the syllabus. He became a mentor and opened the door to an unpaid internship at one of the world's top talent agencies, which she describes in granular period detail: handwritten priorities on yellow legal pads, script coverage read on a StairMaster, headshots stapled to resumes, no project management software and no AI to summarise anything. What she takes from it is a set of capabilities that no course delivered, including how to negotiate, how to prioritise and how to follow through while exhausted. Offered a full-time assistant role before graduating, she declined, having seen enough of the industry to know the game was not hers. The argument broadens into a claim about education generally: the degree and the education are separable, and education comes from what you say yes to, throw yourself into and learn from failing at. She applies the same standard to hiring, valuing demonstrated experience and repetition over credentials, and notes that the cultural penalty for skipping college has softened.
points: Mulder separates the degree from the education, arguing that what shaped her was unpaid, uncredited and outside any syllabus, which makes the essay a claim about where learning actually happens.
The mentor's value lay in teaching how to write, think and market in the real world rather than in covering content, an implicit argument for expertise plus access over curriculum coverage.
Her hiring criteria follow directly from her own history: experience, results and the repetitive reps someone is willing to do, rather than credentials.
The period details, script coverage by hand and no tool to summarise a storyline, quietly make the case that the judgement she was building is exactly the capability now most easily outsourced.
She resists prescribing a single path, noting that some admired leaders dropped out, some used their degrees well, and some finished and found it was not the route they expected.
quotes: His class changed everything for me. Not because it followed the curriculum, but because it didn’t.
He taught us how to write, how to think, and how to market in the real world. He became a mentor to me.
Still, that internship gave me everything I needed to know. It was the first time I saw the power of saying yes before you're ready. The power of showing up, even when you don’t feel like it.
Because the truth is, it’s not always about the degree. It’s about the education. And education doesn’t just come from classrooms.
When I hire someone, I don’t care about the degree. I care about the experience.
Once upon a time, if you didn’t have a college plan after high school, people looked at you like you were messing up your life (some still do).
Some of the most successful leaders I admire dropped out of college and dove straight into the work, the real-world experience and that became their education.
